l: Lilæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lilæa is an ancient town in Phocis, below Parnassus on the route from Delphi, a winter day’s journey from Delphi and about 60 stades from Amphiclea. Named, by local tradition, for Lilæa the Naiad, it holds that Castalia is supplied by Cephisus. Its air is salubrious in spring, summer, and autumn, but cold in winter. Once taken and razed, it was restored, then besieged by Philip the son of Demetrius. After Patron led younger citizens in revolt, the Macedonian garrison left; Lilæa honored him with a statue at Delphi. It has a theatre, market-place, baths, and temples to Apollo and Artemis.

l: Hyettus the Argive, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hyettus the Argive fled Argos after killing Molurus, whom he caught with his wife. Orchomenus received him and granted him the land around the village of Hyettus and its neighboring district. He is presented as the first to take vengeance for adultery.

l: river Platanius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_outlet_into sea The river Platanius has its outlet into the sea below Corsea. The town of Halæ lies on its right near the sea, where the Bœotians border Locris and Eubœa.

l: Antigone, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: drags Polynices’ corpse [until she could throw it onto Eteocles’ blazing funeral pile] Antigone could not easily lift Polynices’s corpse, so she dragged it until she could throw it onto the funeral pile of Eteocles. The place where she did this is called Antigone’s Dragging-ground.

l: temple of the Cabiri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of the Cabiri is an exceptionally holy place about seven stades from the grove of Cabirian Demeter and Proserpine. It destroys hostile or profane entrants: some of Xerxes’ army went mad and died, and Macedonians during Alexander’s attack on Thebes were killed by lightning. It also marks surrounding landmarks and routes.

l: Cabirian mysteries, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Cabirian mysteries, a gift from Demeter to the Cabiri, ceased after the Argives expelled them, then Pelarge and Isthmiades restored them; their rites and originating deposit remain undisclosed.

l: Prometheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: fashioned human race [from clay, according to local belief] Prometheus is identified by some as the figure represented by a Pentelican marble statue in a building at Panopeus. Stones near the ravine, resembling clay and smelling like the human body, are said to be remains of the clay from which Prometheus fashioned the human race.

l: Pelarge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pelarge, daughter of Potneus and wife of Isthmiades, taught and reestablished the Cabirian mysteries, extending their celebration beyond ancient boundaries; after an oracle from Dodona, she received honors and a pregnant sacrificial victim.

l: Naupactus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Naupactus was a town near Œanthea, named in tradition for the fleet built there by the Dorians and sons of Aristomachus to cross to the Peloponnese. It passed from the Locrians to the Athenians, then the Messenians, and back to the Locrians after the Lacedæmonians expelled the Messenians. It had sanctuaries of Poseidon, Artemis, Aphrodite, and ruined Æsculapius, and Phalysius was cured there of blindness.

l: plain of Tenerus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The plain of Tenerus, right of the temple of the Cabiri, is named for Tenerus, a seer considered Apollo and Melia's son.

l: temple to Hercules surnamed Hippodetes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A large temple to Hercules surnamed Hippodetes stands near the plain of Tenerus, commemorating Hercules taking and tethering the Orchomenians' horses by night.

l: mountain of the Sphinx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a mountain The mountain of the Sphinx lies a little beyond the temple to Hercules Hippodetes. The Sphinx is said to have used it as her headquarters or as a base for her robberies.

l: Sphinx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sphinx is associated with the mountain of the Sphinx, where she recites a riddle that ruins captives. Another account calls her a pirate: she sails with a naval force, uses Anthedon as a port, and occupies the mountain for robberies. Called Laius’s illegitimate daughter, she is killed by Œdipus after his Corinthian force defeats her.

l: riddle of the Sphinx, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_used_for ruin of captured people The riddle of the Sphinx was recited to those she captured and brought about their ruin.

l: oracle given to Cadmus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: At Delphi, an oracle given to Cadmus was known only to Theban kings; the Sphinx used it to test Laius’s alleged sons.

l: Onchestus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_named_after Onchestus the son of Poseidon [according to local tradition] Onchestus is described as the son of Poseidon and as the inhabitant of the place whose ruins stand about 15 stades from the mountain of the Sphinx. In the time of the narrator, a statue of Onchestian Poseidon and the grove mentioned by Homer remained there.

l: Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thespia is a town under Mount Helicon, named in differing accounts for Thespia, daughter of Asopus, or Thespius. Its notable features are temples, statues, a theatre, and a market-place worth seeing, including an old stone Eros and statues of Zeus Soter, Dionysus, Fortune, Hygiea, Athene the Worker, and Plutus. Its Eros by Praxiteles went to Rome, returned under Claudius, was removed by Nero, and burned.

l: Helicon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Helicon is a fertile, tree-filled mountain in Greece, sacred to the Muses. Its purslane feeds goats, its grass and roots are harmless to people, and its pastures weaken snake venom. At its foot lies Ascra; on the way to the Muses’ grove are Aganippe, Eupheme’s image, and Linus’s statue. Its summit holds Hippocrene and Lamus, while its grove and festival site are linked with the Thespians and traditions of Hesiod, the Muses, Eros, and Narcissus.

l: statue of Zeus Soter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: At Thespia, a brazen statue of Zeus Soter commemorates Zeus’s attributed rescue from a dragon that once infested the town.

l: dragon of Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: infests Thespia [formerly] The dragon of Thespia once infested the town and was given one youth chosen by lot each year. It was killed when Cleostratus, wearing a specially made breastplate, gave himself to it.

l: Cleostratus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a_victim_of dragon of Thespia [the last victim] Cleostratus was the last victim chosen for the dragon of Thespia. He willingly gave himself to the dragon while wearing the breastplate made by Menestratus, knowing that he would die but also kill the monster.

l: Menestratus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Menestratus, lover of Cleostratus, devises a hooked brazen breastplate that enables Cleostratus to kill the dragon.

l: brazen breastplate with hooks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Menestratus made a brazen breastplate with inward-bent hooks for Cleostratus, enabling him to kill the dragon though he would perish.

l: Eros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Eros is a god especially worshipped at Thespia and by the Pariani. His origin is disputed: most call him Aphrodite's son, Olen names Ilithyia, while Hesiod places him after Chaos, Earth, and Tartarus. Considered by most men the latest god, he received renowned statues and poetic celebration.

l: statue of Eros by Menodorus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_an_imitation_of Praxiteles The statue of Eros by Menodorus stood at Thespia in the author's day. Menodorus, an Athenian, made it as an imitation of Praxiteles's statue.

l: temple of Hercules at Thespia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple has a priestess bound to lifelong virginity. A tradition links this to Hercules sparing a daughter of Thestius, but its possible greater antiquity suggests it may have been erected for Hercules of the Idæan Dactyli.

l: snakes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Snakes on Helicon are said to have less potent venom because of the mountain’s pastures. Wild snakes generally have venom that is deadly to both humans and animals.

l: venom, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Venom belongs to snakes on Helicon and is generally deadly to men and animals when from wild snakes; its strength varies with snakes’ pastures, being weaker in Helicon, stronger in mountainous Phœnicia, and milder near Arabian balsam trees.

l: vipers, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Vipers in mountainous Phœnicia are said to have especially dangerous venom. In Arabia, vipers live and lodge beneath balsam trees, rejoice in their shade, and, feeding on sweet-scented sap, have nondeadly venom despite steel-like bites.

l: balsam trees, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Balsam trees in Arabia are myrtle-bush-sized trees with marjoram-like leaves; vipers lodge beneath their shade and feed on their sap.

l: sap of the balsam tree, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sap of the balsam tree is a sweet-scented ointment and vipers’ preferred food; as nearby vipers feed on it, their venom is said to become milder.

l: Arabians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Arabians gather balsam sap in season, knocking poles to frighten sacred vipers away rather than killing them.

l: Ascra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ascra was a settlement at Helicon’s foot, built by figures named in differing accounts; by the author’s time, only a tower remained.

l: Eurydice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a_wife_of Æneas [according to Lescheos and the author of the Cyprian Poems] According to one account, Eurydice died before Orpheus, who went to Aornus in Thesprotia to consult an oracle of the dead about her. He thought her soul would follow him, but lost her when he turned back to look at her.

l: Dium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The people of Dium say that Orpheus was slain in their region and that his remains were kept there after being removed from Libethra. They also say that the river Helicon went underground so that the women who killed Orpheus could not wash away their blood-guiltiness.

l: Libethra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_destroyed_by Sus [its walls, temples, and houses are swept away] Libethra was a city on Olympus where, according to an account heard at Larissa, Orpheus’s tomb was located nearby. Its people received an oracle that the city would be destroyed when the Sun saw Orpheus’s bones, and Libethra was later destroyed after his urn was broken and his remains were exposed.

l: Orpheus's tomb, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orpheus’s tomb is placed in Pieria or near Libethra; a shepherd’s sleep-song draws a crowd that overturns its pillar, breaks and exposes its urn.

l: stone urn containing Orpheus's remains, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains Orpheus's remains A stone urn containing Orpheus’s remains stood on a pillar beside the road from Dium toward the mountain. The pillar was overturned by people gathering around a sleeping shepherd, the urn fell and broke, and the Sun saw the remains.

l: Orpheus's remains, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orpheus’s remains were said to have been kept in a stone urn near his tomb. After the urn was broken and the remains were exposed, Libethra was destroyed; the Macedonians in Dium later removed the remains to their city.

l: oracle of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: prophesies destruction of Libethra [when the Sun should see the bones of Orpheus] The oracle of Dionysus in Thrace warned the people of Libethra that their city would be destroyed when the Sun saw the bones of Orpheus. They disregarded the warning because they thought a boar could not destroy the city.

l: destruction of Libethra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The destruction of Libethra followed the exposure of Orpheus’s remains after his urn was broken. Heavy rain caused the river Sus to sweep away the city’s walls, temples, and houses and to drown its people and animals.

l: Orphic Hymns, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Hymns of Orpheus are very short, few compositions known and chanted by the Lycomidae at the Mysteries; prized chiefly for religious spirit, they rank second to the Hymns of Homer in composition.

l: mysteries of the gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orpheus was thought to have invented the mysteries of the gods, along with purifications from unholy deeds, cures for diseases, and means of turning away the wrath of the gods.

l: Orpheus's singing, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orpheus’s singing is represented at Helicon by animals listening to him. A shepherd later sang some of Orpheus’s verses aloud in his sleep, drawing shepherds and husbandmen together and causing them to overturn the pillar beside Orpheus’s tomb.

l: the death of Orpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Different traditions say that Orpheus was killed by Thracian women, struck by lightning from the god for revealing things in the mysteries, or that he slew himself from grief after losing Eurydice. The Macedonians of Pieria say that women killed him there.

l: Orpheus's journey to the underworld, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_supposed_to_reach Hades [alive, to recover Eurydice; a belief the author rejects] The Greeks are said to believe that Orpheus went down alive to Hades to recover Eurydice from the gods of the lower world. Another account says that he went to Aornus in Thesprotia to consult an oracle of the dead about Eurydice after her death.

l: Priapus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Priapus is represented by a statue at Mount Helicon, considered well worth seeing. He is especially honoured where sheep, goats, or bees abound, and the people of Lampsacus honour him more than all gods, saying Dionysus and Aphrodite are his parents.

l: Hippocrene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a spring [formed by the horse of Bellerophon striking the earth with its hoof, according to tradition] Hippocrene is a spring reached after ascending twenty stades from the grove at Helicon. It is said to have been formed when the horse of Bellerophon struck the earth with its hoof, and lead bearing The Works and Days was reportedly found near it.

l: The Works and Days, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: begins_at Strife [according to the Bœotians, who remove the address to the Muses] The Works and Days is attributed by some people at Helicon as the only work written by Hesiod, with its opening address to the Muses removed so that it begins with the section about Strife. A lead copy of the poem was shown near Hippocrene, though it was almost entirely rotten with age.

l: Narcissus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Narcissus, said to love his nearly identical twin sister, is associated with a fountain where traditions say he died of love after mistaking his reflection for another person; another says, after her death, he imagined her image there. A flower depicts him but predates the Thespian Narcissus.

l: Creusis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Creusis is a haven of the Thespians with no public monuments; a private house holds a painted plaster Dionysus statue, and its sea approach is circuitous and rough from promontories and mountain winds.

l: Thisbe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thisbe is a coastal city in Bœotia beyond a coastal mountain and plain. It has a temple and standing stone statue of Hercules, for whom its inhabitants celebrate a festival. A strong embankment and annual water diversion keep the plain from becoming a lake and allow dry land to be cultivated. The city is said to be named for the local Nymph Thisbe.

l: Tilphusa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tilphusa is a fountain near Mount Tilphusium, about 50 stades from Haliartus, where Tiresias drank, died, and was buried.

l: death of Tiresias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: occurs_at Tilphusa Tiresias’s death occurred at the fountain Tilphusa after he drank from it while thirsty. He was buried at the fountain.

l: Lophis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lophis is a river flowing through Haliartus’s district, said to have gushed from the ground through Lophis’s blood.

l: Lophis (son of the ruler), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lophis, son of Haliartus’s ruler, is killed when his father obeys a Pythian Priestess’s command after seeking water; still living, he runs as water springs where his blood flows, giving the water its name.

l: temple of Athene at Alalcomenae, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Temple near Alalcomenae once contained an old ivory statue of Athene; after Sulla removed it, neglect and ivy caused its stones to detach.

l: old ivory statue of Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_made_of ivory [old] The old ivory statue of Athene stood in her temple near Alalcomenae. Sulla took it away, after which the temple was neglected.

l: Triton, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A small torrent near Alalcomenae, named for Athene’s upbringing beside a river called Triton, is distinguished from Libya’s Triton flowing from Lake Tritonis into the Libyan sea.

l: temple of Itonian Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Itonian Athene, named after Itonus, stands between Alalcomenæ and Coronea on the route to Coronea. It hosts the Bœotians’ general meeting and contains brazen statues of Itonian Athene and Zeus by Agoracritus, plus later statues of the Graces.

l: Andreus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Andreus, son of the river Peneus, first dwells at Orchomenus, whose land is called Andreis; urged by Athamas, he marries Euippe and has Eteocles, and is represented by an armored statue.

l: Almus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Almus, son of Sisyphus, has daughters Chrysogenia and Chryse; after Eteocles dies, his descendants inherit the succession.

l: representation of the Graces, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_dressed dressed representation of the Graces [in more ancient artistic practice] In more ancient times, statuaries and painters represented the Graces dressed. Examples included the golden Graces by Bupalus at Smyrna, a painted Grace by Apelles in the Odeum, Graces by Bupalus in the bed-chamber of Attalus at Pergamus, Graces by the Parian Pythagoras in the Pythium, and statues by Socrates at the entrance to the Acropolis.

l: naked representation of the Graces, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a_later_representation representation of the Graces [artists adopted it afterward] The first person to represent the Graces naked, whether in sculpture or painting, was not known. Artists later changed the representation, and in Pausanias’s time they sculpted and painted the Graces as naked.

l: Phlegyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phlegyas, son of Chryse and Ares, became king after Eteocles died, renamed Andreis’s country and city for himself, gathered warlike Greeks, and died childless.

l: people of Phlegyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The people of Phlegyas separated from the Orchomenians, drew neighboring peoples, and, delighting in war, marched against Delphi to plunder its temple. Defeated by Philammon and some Argives, they were later devastated by lightning, earthquakes, and epidemic; few survivors escaped to Phocis.

l: Minyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Minyas, king of Orchomenus and son of Chryses, gained great wealth through rule; his revenues surpassed earlier rulers’, and he built the first known Treasury for his money. He later had a tomb at Orchomenus, and Orchomenians were called Minyae.

l: Treasury of Minyas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Treasury of Minyas is a remarkable circular stone treasury at Orchomenus, built to receive Minyas’s money. It has a not very pointed top, whose highest stone is said to hold the whole building together. Though Greek historians omitted it, it is called a marvel inferior to nothing in Greece or elsewhere.

l: town of Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: was_called Orchomenus [during the reign of Orchomenus] During the reign of Orchomenus, the town took the name Orchomenus, and its inhabitants took the name Orchomenians. It received Hyettus as a refugee from Argos, and Orchomenus gave him the surrounding land.

l: yearly tax for the murder of Clymenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The yearly tax was imposed on the Thebans after Erginus and his brothers defeated Thebes in retaliation for Clymenus's murder. Hercules later had the tax remitted.

l: Agamedes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Agamedes, son of Erginus and brother of Trophonius, was a skilled builder of temples and palaces; after building and robbing Hyrieus’s treasury, he was trapped and beheaded by Trophonius.

l: Ascalaphus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ascalaphus, reputed son of Ares by Astyoche, rules the Orchomenians with Ialmenus and leads the Minyæ to Troy.

l: Ialmenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ialmenus, reputed son of Ares by Astyoche, jointly ruled the Orchomenians with Ascalaphus and led the Minyæ to Troy.

l: spectre of Actaeon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: At Orchomenus, Actaeon's spectre sat on a stone and injured the land; Orchomenians fastened a brazen copy to it.

l: Chersias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Chersias, an Orchomenian, wrote lost verses on Orchomenus, described Aspledon’s parentage and birth, and was said to have composed an epitaph on Hesiod.

l: Lebadea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lebadea, a town nearest the Orchomenians in the plain, began as high-ground Midea. After Lebadus came from Athens and settled there, its inhabitants descended and renamed it. Adorned like famous Greek towns, it contains Trophonius's oracle, once unfound by Bœotian messengers, and a Dædalus work.

l: Grove of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Grove of Trophonius is a place some distance from Lebadea. Its notable features include the temple of Trophonius, Demeter Europa’s temple, Zeus Hyetius, Proserpine’s Chase, Zeus the King’s temple, temples of Cronos, Hera, Zeus, and Apollo, and Arcesilaus’s tomb.

l: River Hercyna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: River Hercyna springs from a cave when Proserpine takes a stone while retrieving a goose; its cave sources and bank temple, where oracle seekers bathe, center on a maiden-and-goose effigy.

l: Temple of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_statue statue of Trophonius [like Æsculapius] The temple of Trophonius is among the principal features of the grove. It contains a statue like Æsculapius, made by Praxiteles.

l: oracle of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle of Trophonius is a small circular walled enclosure above the grove on the mountain, with brazen pillars, girders, and doors. It contains an artificial, oven-shaped chamber; a consulter enters its narrow opening lying flat, offering feet, knees, body, and honey cakes.

l: Temple of the Good Deity and Good Fortune, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_residence_for oracle consultation and descent [during preparatory days] A person seeking the oracle must first stay for several days in the temple of the Good Deity and Good Fortune. After returning from the sanctuary, the person is brought back there while still terrified and confused, and later is said to recover and laugh about the experience.

l: sacrificial ritual for Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: requires_sacrifices_to Trophonius [and several other deities] Before descending, the consulter purifies himself, avoids warm baths, bathes in the River Hercyna, and receives animal food from various victims. Sacrifices are made to Trophonius and his sons, Apollo, Cronos, Zeus the King, Hera the Chariot-driver, and Demeter called Europa, with a seer inspecting the entrails; on the night of descent, a ram is sacrificed in a ditch while Agamedes is invoked, and its entrails must be favorable.

l: oracle consultation and descent, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An oracle consultation and descent requires a ram sacrifice with favourable entrails. Two thirteen-year-old Hermæ attendants prepare the consulter, who drinks Lethe to forget and Memory to remember, worships a statue, and enters at night. Inside, the future is communicated by sight or hearing; afterward priests use the Seat of Memory, question the consulter, and record the account on a tablet.

l: the drought, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The drought lasted for two years without rain, leading the Bœotians to consult Delphi and seek a cure from Trophonius.

l: the oracle of Trophonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle was discovered when Saon from Acræphnium followed a swarm of bees into the ground. Saon was then instructed in its ritual and routine by Trophonius.

l: Saon from Acræphnium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Saon, oldest of the Bœotian messengers, follows bees underground to discover Trophonius’s oracle at Lebadea, then learns its ritual and routine from Trophonius.

l: Taxilus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Taxilus, the general of Mithridates, attacked Elatea, but the Elateans held out against him. Their resistance to Taxilus and the barbarians from Pontus led the Romans to grant them freedom and immunity from taxation.

l: the common sepulchre of the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The common sepulchre at Chæronea held Thebans killed against Philip; uninscribed, it bore a lion monument, perhaps signifying their bravery.

l: sceptre of Agamemnon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The sceptre of Agamemnon, a probably sole surviving work of Hephæstus, was made for Zeus and passed through Hermes, Pelops, Atreus, and Thyestes to Agamemnon. Found in Phocis on the Panopeans’ borders, it was Chæronea’s most venerated object: kept in a building, bright with divine properties, and given daily sacrifices and annual food offerings.

l: Amathus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Amathus is a city in Cyprus, notable for its ancient temple of Adonis and Aphrodite, which contains Harmonia’s necklace, called Eriphyle’s.

l: necklace at Amathus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The necklace at Amathus, in the ancient temple of Adonis and Aphrodite, is made of emeralds set in gold. Though said to be Harmonia’s and later Eriphyle’s necklace, the text doubts this because Eriphyle’s was entirely gold.

l: Petrachos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Petrachos is a crag above Chæronea, said to be where Rhea deceived Cronos with a stone instead of Zeus; a small statue of Zeus stands on its summit.

l: unguents made at Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Chæronea unguents, made by boiling lilies, roses, narcissuses, and irises, relieve pain; rose unguent also preserves anointed wooden statues from rottenness.

l: Hyampolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hyampolis was an ancient town, founded by Hyantes who fled Thebes and originally called the town of the Hyantes. It mattered as a Phocian defensive site against Thessalian cavalry and through Daiphantes. Xerxes burnt it and Philip razed it, yet it retained a market-place, council-chamber, theatre, and Adrian’s Portico, relying on one well and winter rainwater.

l: Abæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Abæ is a Phocian town, said to have been founded by Abas and settled by people from Argos. Sacred to Apollo, it had an oracle, theatre, and market-place. It avoided impiety, temple seizure, and the Phocian or Sacred War, and Romans granted it autonomy for Apollo’s sake.

l: earthenware pots, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: disables Thessalian cavalry [by laming horses and causing riders to be killed or unhorsed] The Phocians buried earthenware pots in the ground at the place where they expected the Thessalian cavalry to attack. The pots lamed some horses and caused some Thessalian riders to be killed or thrown from their horses.

l: Thessalian cavalry, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thessalian cavalry charged over the concealed earthenware pots at Hyampolis, suffering lamed horses, killed riders, and men who were unhorsed. It later helped kill Gelon and the 300 picked Phocians.

l: oracle concerning the Phocians' danger, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_given_by Apollo [at Delphi] The oracle said that a mortal and an immortal would be put together in combat, with victory given to both but the greater victory to the mortal. It became clear to the Greeks after the Phocians won, because the Thessalian word was Itonian Athene and the Phocian word was Phocus.

l: Gelon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Gelon commands 300 picked Phocians on a nocturnal mission against the Thessalians, ordered to avoid fighting; the Thessalians kill him and all his men in battle.

l: Phocian women and children, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: are_placed_under_guard_at funeral pile [with the Phocians' goods and valuables] The Phocians gathered their women and children before the decisive battle. They ordered that, if the Phocians were defeated, the women and children should be killed and offered as victims.

l: funeral pile, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains Phocian women and children [as part of the Phocians' desperate resolution] The Phocians built a large funeral pile containing their gathered possessions, including apparel, gold, silver, and statues of the gods. Thirty men were ordered to kill the women and children, burn the pile, and either kill one another or attack the Thessalian cavalry if the Phocians lost.

l: Tellias of Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tellias of Elis, the Phocians’ seer and commander in chief, bore their hopes for safety, helped secure victory, and devised their plaster-disguised night attack.

l: battle between the Phocians and Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_commander Tellias of Elis [commander in chief of the Phocians] The battle was commanded for the Phocians by Rhœus of Ambrosus and Daiphantes of Hyampolis, with Tellias of Elis as commander in chief. The Phocians fought in desperation after preparing for the possible destruction of their women, children, and possessions, and they won a famous victory.

l: Phocian victory over the Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_won_by Phocians [in one of the most famous victories of their time] The Phocians' victory was aided by their desperation and by auspicious omens from the god. They commemorated it by sending statues of Tellias, the other commanders, and local heroes to Apollo at Delphi.

l: night attack on the Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: causes Thessalians [a tremendous slaughter] Five hundred picked Phocians launched the night attack when the moon was full after the Thessalian camp had been pitched at the entrance to Phocis. They covered themselves and their armour with plaster so that they looked white, causing a tremendous slaughter because the Thessalians mistook them for a divine appearance.

l: Philomelus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Philomelus, a Ledonian son of Philotimus and second in merit among the Phocians, took a golden shield, urged seizure of Delphi's temple over an unpaid fine, led war against the Thebans, and died after defeat near Neon.

l: Ledon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ledon was formerly a town, named in local tradition after the Autochthon Ledon. Destroyed because of Philomelus's impiety and later deserted for weakness, it survived only in name: about 80 inhabitants lived by the Cephisus in a settlement called Ledon.

l: temple at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_located_at Delphi The Phocians seized the temple at Delphi after Philomelus persuaded them that they could not pay their fine. The seizure led to war with the Thebans, and the Amphictyonic Council condemned those who plundered the temple to the same end as Philomelus.

l: war between the Phocians and the Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: lasts 10 continuous years The war lasted ten continuous years, during which the Phocians and their mercenaries and the Thebans repeatedly prevailed over one another. The conflict turned against the Phocians in an engagement near Neon, where they were routed.

l: Onomarchus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Onomarchus, brother of Phayllus, became Phocian commander after Philomelus’s death, was defeated by Philip allied with the Thebans, fled, and was killed by his own soldiers.

l: Phayllus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phayllus becomes the Phocians’ commander in chief with unlimited power after Onomarchus dies, then dreams of becoming a wasting brass old man among Apollo’s offerings and soon suffers the foretold wasting disease.

l: Phalæcus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phalæcus, son of Phayllus, gained chief power in Phocis after his father died. He was deposed for privately taking sacred money, then went to Crete with supporters and mercenaries. Besieging Cydonia for money, he lost most of his army and died.

l: Parapotamii, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Parapotamii was an ancient town in Phocis, renowned in ancient times. Xerxes burned and destroyed it; it was not restored by the Athenians and Boeotians. Its impoverished inhabitants were distributed among other towns, and by the author's day no ruins remained and its site was unknown.

l: Panopeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Panopeus is an ancient town in Phocis, about twenty stades from Chæronea. Though renowned and represented on the Phocian Council, it lacks major civic amenities; its people live in narrow dwellings by a ravine within an ancient enclosure. Accounts connect it with Epeus’s father or Phlegyans from Orchomenia. Its enclosure served against the Bœotians, and Thyiades’ dances may explain Homer’s name for it. It was later taken and razed.

l: Daulis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Daulis is an ancient town in Phocis, about seven stades from Panopeus, though the distance may be corrupt. Despite few inhabitants, it is renowned among the Phocians for size and strength. It was said to be named for the nymph Daulis or for former dense trees, and was traditionally associated with the first cannibalism among mankind. It has a temple of Athene, an older wooden statue brought by Procne, and Tronis with a hero-chapel. From Daulis, routes lead up Parnassus and along the high road to Delphi; after being taken, it was razed to the ground.

l: Charadra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Charadra is a settlement on a lofty ridge about 20 stades beyond Lilæa. Its chief constraint is scarce water, supplied only by the Charadrus three stades downhill, while its chief advantage is the best planting, sowing, and pasture land near the Cephisus. Its market-place has altars to Heroes of Charadra.

l: Amphiclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Amphiclea, 60 stades from Lilæa, was also called Amphicæa and locally Ophitea. Its inhabitants linked it to a snake that protected a child but was killed with him. Its most notable observances were secret Dionysian orgies, an oracle through dreams, prophetic possession of the priest, and dream cures for sickness.

l: Drymæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Drymæa, originally called Nauboles, lies beyond Tithronium and from Amphiclea. Local tradition names Phocus the son of Æacus as founder. Its chief feature is an ancient temple to Law-giving Demeter, with a stone statue honored annually at the Thesmophoria.

l: Medeon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: plundered temple at Delphi [impiously] Medeon lies in ruins above Anticyra. It was one of the towns that impiously plundered the temple at Delphi.

l: Stiris, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Stiris is a town on high, rocky ground, said to have been founded by Athenians who came from Attica with Peteus after his expulsion from Athens, and named after Stiria. Its few wells give poor water, so it uses a rock-hewn spring below. It has a temple and ancient statue of Demeter and begins the road to Ambrosus.

l: general Council of the Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Some people say that Amphictyon, the son of Deucalion, appointed the general Council of the Greeks. Androtion instead says that delegates originally came to Delphi from neighboring people called Amphictiones.

l: Phocian towns, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phocian towns, including Lilæa, Hyampolis, Anticyra, Parapotamii, Panopeus, and Daulis, were taken and razed after war, turned into villages except Abæ, then rebuilt and repopulated, though some remained weak for lack of money.

l: irruption of the Galati into Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_greatest_struggle_at Delphi [between the Galati and the Greeks] The irruption included an earlier expedition under Cambaules, a second expedition in which Bolgius fought the Macedonians and Illyrians, and a major invasion led by Brennus and Acichorius. The greatest struggle of this invasion against the Greeks took place at Delphi.

l: Phocian General Council, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Phocian authorities were among those who enriched themselves most and longest from the treasures of the god at Delphi.

l: Tityus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tityus is a wounded figure in a picture near the treasury of the Sicyonians, worn by continuous punishment to a shadow. He is associated with a sepulchre near the ravine at Panopeus. Homer describes him across nine roods, though this may name where he lay.

l: Thyiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thyiades are Athenian women named after Thyia, who annually travel with Delphian women to Parnassus to celebrate Dionysus. Along the way and at places including Panopeus, they hold dances; on Mount Parnassus they conduct mad revels honoring Dionysus and Apollo.

l: Cross-roads, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cross-roads, where three roads meet, is said to be where Oedipus murdered his father; tombs of Laius and his attendant stand at its center.

l: oracle of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle of Apollo at Delphi has competing accounts of its origins and succession: it was previously oracle of Earth, jointly linked with Poseidon and Earth, and reportedly set up by Olen. Phemonoe was its first priestess in the widespread tradition. Later, it rejected Themistocles’ Persian spoils and ordered them removed from the temple and sent home.

l: first temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: was_built_of laurel [branches brought from a tree at Tempe] The first temple of Apollo is said to have been built from laurel branches brought from a tree at Tempe, making it resemble a hut.

l: fourth temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The fourth temple of Apollo, a stone building by Trophonius and Agamedes, was built and then burned down under Erxiclides in the first year of the 58th Olympiad.

l: Parnassus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Parnassus, a hero and son of the Nymph Cleodora, is said to have Poseidon as divine father and Cleopompus as human father. He built Lycorea, discovered bird-flight omens, and gave his name to Mount Parnassus and dell Parnassus.

l: Deucalion’s flood, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: destroyed Lycorea [according to the tradition about the town built by Parnassus] Deucalion’s flood is said to have destroyed the town built by Parnassus. The human beings who escaped the flood followed wolves and other wild beasts to Mount Parnassus and founded Lycorea.

l: Lycorea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lycorea, a town later called Delphi and Pytho, was supposedly founded by survivors of Deucalion’s flood who followed wolves to Mount Parnassus; its name meant Wolf-town, though another tradition named it for Lycorus.

l: Corycian cavern, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Corycian cavern, on Mount Parnassus, is named after the Nymph Corycia and is considered more remarkable than the other described caverns. Much of it can be traversed without torches; it has a high roof, springs, bubbling water, and roof-drip. Its inhabitants hold it sacred to Pan and the Corycian Nymphs.

l: Pytho, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pytho was another name used by the inhabitants for Delphi, a town. Genealogists linked its name to Pythes, while prevalent tradition tied it to a dragon slain by Apollo that rotted there.

l: dragon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Earth placed dragon to guard her oracle; Apollo slew it with arrows, and its rotting was said to give Pytho its name.

l: Delphians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Delphians are a group associated with accounts of Herophile’s oracles from a projecting stone above Delphi. They begged Apollo for protection, then followed a divinely directed wolf, recovered stolen sacred gold, and dedicated a bronze wolf to the god.

l: oracle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_in hexameters The dragon was said to guard Earth’s oracle before Apollo slew it. When the Delphians sought Apollo’s protection from a plundering son of Crius, Phemonoe, who was then priestess, delivered an oracle in hexameters promising that Apollo would send his heavy arrow against the man.

l: temple at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple at Delphi was repeatedly plundered: first by an Eubœan robber, then the people of Phlegyas, Pyrrhus son of Achilles, Xerxes’ army, the Phocian authorities and Galati most extensively, and finally Nero, who carried off 500 bronze statues from Apollo.

l: Neoptolemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, is also called Pyrrhus and was named by Phœnix because he was very young when he first went to war. He is chiefly remembered as a relentless Greek killer of Trojans: he killed Eioneus, Coroebus, Priam, and Agenor, and is depicted killing Elasus and striking Astynous. He was the only Greek shown continuing to butcher Trojans. He was slain by Apollo’s priest at an altar in Delphi; his grave lies beside the temple, where Delphi’s people annually give him funeral rites.

l: musical contest at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_original_contest singing a Hymn in honour of Apollo [the most ancient contest and first prize contest] The earliest contest at Delphi was a musical contest for singing a hymn in honour of Apollo. Later, contests were established for harping, pipes, singing to the pipes, and harping without vocal accompaniment.

l: singing a Hymn in honour of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Singing a Hymn in honour of Apollo, Delphi’s most ancient prize contest, began with Chrysothemis the Cretan as reported victor, followed by Philammon and his son Thamyris.

l: singing to the pipes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Singing to the pipes became a Pythian contest in the third year of the 48th Olympiad, when Echembrotus of Arcadia won; it was discontinued in the second Pythiad as gloomy music associated with elegies and dirges.

l: chariot race, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_victor Clisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon A chariot race was later added to the Pythian contests, and Clisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon was proclaimed its victor. The games subsequently included races for a pair-horse chariot, a chariot with colts, a pair of colts, and a racing colt.

l: crown of laurel, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Crown of laurel is awarded to Pythian games victors, probably because Apollo was reportedly enamoured of Daphne, daughter of Ladon.

l: Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Brennus is a Celtic leader and strategist who instigates and commands the Galatian invasion of Greece alongside Acichorius. He persuades Galatian assemblies and chieftains to invade by stressing Greek weakness and the wealth of communities and temples, then is chosen commander. He directs a large barbarian army with a bodyguard of its finest and boldest men, showing tactical skill by sending 10,000 tall, able-swimming troops across the Sperchius at a weakly guarded marsh, ordering bridges built, and advancing toward Heraclea and Thermopylæ. Seeking to isolate the Ætolians, he appoints Orestorius and Combutis to lead an expedition into Ætolia, uses Ænianes and Heracleans as guides through Mount Œta, and leaves Acichorius with the main army at Thermopylæ while he marches on Delphi. Wounded in the battle at Delphi and carried away unconscious, he later kills himself by drinking neat wine, from fear of or shame before his comrades.

l: Locrians called Ozolæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Locrians around Amphissa, Myonia, Œanthea, and Naupactus; Amphissa was largest, others granted to Achæans of Patræ, and its inhabitants joined Ætolians ashamed of “Ozolian.”

l: temple of Athene Pronoia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains Athene Pronoia [within the temple; the ante-chapel has a larger statue] The temple of Athene Pronoia was the fourth of four temples encountered on entering Delphi. Its ante-chapel contained a large brass statue offered by the Massaliotes, while the golden shield offered by Crœsus had been removed, according to the Delphians, by Philomelus.

l: Massaliotes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Massaliotes were colonists of the Phocæans in Ionia, descended from refugees fleeing Phocæa from Harpagus the Mede. They later defeated the Carthaginians at sea, prospered, and offered a large brass statue to Athene Pronoia for victory.

l: Phocæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: fled_from Phocæa [from Harpagus the Mede] The Phocæans in Ionia founded the Massaliotes’ colony. Some of them had fled Phocæa from Harpagus the Mede before the Massaliotes defeated the Carthaginians and obtained the land they occupied.

l: Carthaginians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Carthaginians built Caralis and Sulci in Sardinia, became a great naval power, subdued nearly all Sardinians, allied with Libyans or Iberes, while mountains protected Ilians and Corsi from slavery.

l: river Plistus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The river Plistus flowed through Cirrha until Solon diverted it, added hellebore roots, then restored its course, causing drinkers to suffer incessant diarrhoea.

l: Castalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Castalia is a drinkable spring on the road from the gymnasium to the temple at Delphi. Its origin and name are disputed: attributed to a local woman or Castalius, called Achelous’s daughter by Panyasis, and supplied by Cephisus according to Alcæus and Lilæa’s people.

l: Cephisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cephisus is a roaring current that rises at Lilæa, flows powerfully near Ledon, especially at midday, and nourishes land described as Phocis’s best for planting, sowing, and pasture.

l: invasion of Delphi by Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: occurs_in Phocis In the battle of Delphi, Brennus’s Galati fought the Greeks while earthquakes, thunder, lightning, and falling rocks disrupted them. The Greeks attacked from the front and rear, and the Galati retreated after Brennus was wounded.

l: sacred precincts of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Very large sacred precincts of Apollo in upper Delphi, entered several ways, contain numerous votive offerings, including statues dedicated by Corcyræans, Tegeans, and Lacedæmonians.

l: votive offerings, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a offerings [at Delphi] The votive offerings at Delphi include Phayllus of Croton, a bronze bull dedicated by the Corcyræans, statues commemorating Tegean spoils from the Lacedæmonians, and statues dedicated by the Lacedæmonians after defeating the Athenians. Other offerings commemorate the Spartans and their allies at Ægos-potamoi, as well as the Argives’ claimed victory beyond Thyrea.

l: Aegospotami battle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Aegospotami battle was fought by Spartans, allies, and Lysander against Athenians; after victory, Lacedæmonians dedicated Delphi statues, while Athenians attributed their defeat to Lysander bribing admirals Tydeus and Adimantus.

l: Cnidians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: dedicate_statues_to Delphi The Cnidians brought statues to Delphi, including Triopas standing by a horse and Leto, Apollo, and Artemis shooting at the wounded Tityus. They were also the founders or colonists associated with Lipara, and their leader was said to have been Pentathlus.

l: statues dedicated from the tenth of the spoils of Marathon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Statues made by Phidias included Athene and Apollo; later Antigonus, Demetrius, and Ptolemy were sent to Delphi.

l: Tarentum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tarentum, named after Taras and shared with a river, is a maritime city, greatest and most prosperous among barbarian-held Italian cities, captured by Phalanthus after he understood a Delphic oracle.

l: Æthra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_the_mother_of Theseus Æthra, the mother of Theseus, is depicted next to Helen with her head shaven. Lescheos says that she escaped when Ilium was taken, reached the Greek camp, and was recognized by the sons of Theseus; Demophon asked Agamemnon for her, and Helen consented to release her.

l: foundation of Tarentum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tarentum was founded through the Lacedæmonian colonization led by Phalanthus. The city and its river were said to have received their names from the hero Taras, who was the son of Poseidon and a local Nymph.

l: treasury of the Sicyonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The treasury of the Sicyonians stands near the Tarentines’ offering, contains no money, and has Cnidian statues beside it.

l: Siphnian treasury, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a treasury The Siphnian treasury was built after the god instructed the Siphnii to send a tenth of the revenue from Siphnos's gold mines to Delphi. The Siphnii sent this tenth until they ceased the tribute in their cupidity.

l: Siphnii, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Siphnii built a treasury and sent mine revenue to Delphi, but ceased tribute in cupidity; the sea then swept away their gold mines.

l: Siphnos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has gold mines of Siphnos Siphnos had gold mines whose revenue supported the Siphnii's tribute to Delphi and the construction of the Siphnian treasury. The sea later encroached on the island and destroyed the mines after the tribute was discontinued.

l: Lipara, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lipara, a Cnidian city-colony led by Pentathlus, was occupied by colonists; its people later defeated Tyrrhenians at sea and erected statues.

l: Tyrrhenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Tyrrhenians sailed against the Liparæans with five ships, thinking themselves a match for them. Their first fleet and three additional groups of five ships were captured by the Liparæans.

l: Athenian portico, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Athenian portico was built with money obtained by Athenians in war against Peloponnesians and Greek allies; nearby votive captured-ship figure-heads and brazen shields named the cities supplying spoil.

l: naval victories of the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Athenians commemorated their naval victories with figure-heads of captured ships, brazen shields, and sacrifices to Theseus and Poseidon at the promontory of Rhium. The inscription lists Elis, Lacedæmon, Sicyon, Megara, Pellene in Achaia, Ambracia, Leucas, and Corinth among the cities connected with the spoil.

l: second Herophile, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The second Herophile is a Sibyl who lived before the Trojan War and foretold Helen’s upbringing in Sparta, the ruin of Asia Minor and Europe, and the Greek capture of Ilium. In verses spoken while possessed, she called herself Artemis and described herself as Apollo’s wife and sibling. Her origins were variously linked to a mortal sire, Nymphs, Mount Ida, Marpessus, Corycus, and Theodorus; Erythræ strongly claimed her. She lived chiefly at Samos, chanted at Delphi, and was associated with Clarus and Delos. After death in the Troad, she was buried in the grove of Sminthian Apollo, whose sacristan she was said to be.

l: Phaennis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phaennis is a divinely inspired prophetess, daughter of the Chaones’ king, contemporary with Antiochus. A generation before the Celts passed into Asia, she foretold their advance and that Attalus, the bull-horned helper, would destroy the Galati.

l: Marpessus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Marpessus, the second Herophile’s native place and sacred to her mother, became ruins on Trojan Ida, retaining about sixty inhabitants and lying 240 stades from Alexandria in the Troad.

l: Troad, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The second Herophile died in the Troad, where her tomb was located in the grove of Sminthian Apollo. Marpessus, associated with her origins, was also located in the Troad.

l: projecting stone, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a oracle site [according to the Delphians] The projecting stone above Delphi was said by the Delphians to be the place where the first Herophile chanted her oracles. The second Herophile was also said to have stood on this stone when she chanted.

l: oracles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: are_chanted_by second Herophile [at several sacred places] The oracles attributed to the Herophiles included predictions about Helen, the ruin of Asia Minor and Europe, and the capture of Ilium by the Greeks. The text also mentions oracles delivered by Demo and other prophetically inspired figures.

l: divine inspiration, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Divine inspiration was the means by which Phaennis and the Peleae at Dodona prophesied, although they were not called Sibyls. Euclus, Musaeus, Lycus, and Bacis were also said to have been inspired by Nymphs.

l: Pæonian bison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pæonian bison is a beast, most difficult to capture alive. Hunters drive it into a palisaded hollow, make it slip on hides, weaken it by hunger, attract and tame it with husked pinenuts, then bind and lead it away; Dropion sent its brazen head to Delphi.

l: brazen head of the Pæonian bison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A brazen votive offering at Delphi, sent by Dropion, stood opposite a statue of Andreus.

l: golden tripod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: stands_on bronze dragon [as a votive offering at Delphi] The golden tripod was part of the joint Greek offering made after the battle of Platæa. Although the bronze dragon remained at Delphi, the golden part had been abstracted by the Phocian leaders.

l: Tenedian axes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Tenedian axes are a votive offering associated with Periclytus and Tenedos, connected with Tennes cutting Cycnus’s ship ropes, inspiring a proverb for abruptly refusing discussion.

l: Cycnus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cycnus, son of Poseidon and king of Colonæ, has Tennes and Hemithea with Proclea. After second wife Phylonome falsely accuses Tennes, he casts both children into the sea, learns the truth, and sails after Tennes seeking forgiveness.

l: Leucophrys, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Leucophrys, an island, received Tennes and Hemithea safely after they were sent to sea in a chest, then was renamed Tenedos after Tennes.

l: Tennes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tennes, son of Cycnus and Proclea and brother of Hemithea, was falsely accused by Phylonome, cast into the sea, reached Leucophrys, rejected Cycnus’s forgiveness, became associated with Tenedos, and was killed by Achilles defending it.

l: Tenedos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tenedos, formerly Leucophrys, was named from Tennes, inhabited by its people, who were eventually joined to Alexandria because they were weak.

l: spoils of the Medes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: are_offered_to Apollo [by Themistocles] The spoils of the Medes were brought by Themistocles to Delphi as a proposed gift to Apollo. The Pythian Priestess ordered that they not be placed in the temple and that they be sent away as quickly as possible.

l: invasion of Greece by the barbarian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The barbarian's invasion of Greece was foretold in Bacis's oracles and earlier verses by Euclus.

l: bronze wolf, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The bronze wolf, a Delphian votive offering near the great altar, commemorates a wolf that killed a thief of the god’s treasures and led the Delphians to hidden sacred gold.

l: oracle about the Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An oracle foretells that the Galati will cross the Hellespont, devastate Asia, and afflict coastal people, before Cronion raises Attalus as a helper who destroys them.

l: bronze palm and gilt statue of Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Athenians dedicated a bronze palm and gilt statue of Athene at Delphi to commemorate victory at the Eurymedon on land and river; later gold was missing, and crows reportedly damaged its spear, owls, and palm fruit.

l: expedition to Sicily, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_described_as fatal expedition [in Clitodemus's account of the prodigies] The Athenians were preparing for the expedition to Sicily when, according to Clitodemus, an immense number of crows came to Delphi and damaged the statue of Athene and its accompanying objects. Clitodemus related this and other prodigies as warnings against the expedition.

l: votive offerings, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Votive offerings at Delphi, sent to Apollo by Lydian kings, include the surviving iron base of Alyattes’ bowl and other dedications commemorating myths, victories, prosperity, and warfare.

l: iron base of the bowl of Alyattes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The iron base of the bowl of Alyattes is a votive offering made by Glaucus of Chios. The only remaining part of offerings sent by Lydian kings to Apollo, it was welded from iron into a turret-like structure with ladder-like girders and outward-bending bars supporting the bowl.

l: seafight between the Liparæans and Tyrrhenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A seafight between the Liparæans and Tyrrhenians begins after Pythian Priestess instructs a small fleet; five Liparæan triremes capture twenty Tyrrhenian ships.

l: Liparæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Liparæans, following the Pythian Priestess’s instruction, fight the Tyrrhenians with five triremes, capture four groups of five ships, and dedicate matching Apollo statues at Delphi.

l: Sardinians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Sardinians, inhabitants of Sardinia, offered a brazen statue of Sardus and continued honouring Iolaus; their island was eventually conquered by the Carthaginians, except for the Ilians and Corsi.

l: Ilians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Ilians were Trojans who fled the Libyans to Sardinia’s rocky mountains, where protection from Carthaginians preserved their freedom; they remained Ilians and resembled Libyans in appearance, armour, and life.

l: Corsi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: originate_from Corsica [a factional exile contingent settled in Sardinia] The Corsi came from Cyrnus, which the Greeks called Corsica, after a large contingent crossed to Sardinia during factional conflict. They settled in part of Sardinia’s mountainous district and were named after their homeland. Like the Ilians, they avoided enslavement by the Carthaginians because of the security provided by the mountains.

l: Phana, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a fenced village Phana was a fenced village in Ætolia whose inhabitants depended on a small, measured supply of water from a well near the walls. The Achæans captured it after making that water undrinkable.

l: siege of Phana, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: lasts a long time The siege lasted a long time because the Achæans could not take Phana. They learned how to succeed after sending messengers to Delphi and discovering the town’s dependence on one well.

l: oracle concerning the capture of Phana, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An oracle delivered at Delphi to the Achæans directs them to inspect Phana’s water supply and consumption. Though initially misunderstood, it is later applied when the Achæans foul the town’s water.

l: Ambraciotes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Ambraciotes detect a Molossian ambush after an ass disturbance, defeat the Molossi in a night attack, and offer a brazen ass.

l: brazen ass, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a votive offering [of the Ambraciotes] The Ambraciotes offered a brazen ass after their night victory over the Molossi.

l: Molossi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: prepare night attack of the Molossi [against the Ambraciotes] The Molossi prepared a night attack on the Ambraciotes. They were dismayed by the braying and disorderly noise of an ass and its driver, left their ambush, and were defeated.

l: night attack of the Molossi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_disrupted_by ass in the Molossian ambush [when the ass pursued a she-ass and brayed] The night attack was prepared by the Molossi against the Ambraciotes. An ass pursuing a she-ass disrupted the ambush, allowing the Ambraciotes to detect the plan and defeat them that night.

l: ass in the Molossian ambush, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The ass was being driven from the field when it pursued a she-ass with lust and brayed, while its driver shouted loudly and disorderly. The disturbance frightened the Molossi out of their ambush and contributed to their defeat.

l: Olympiodorus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: rendered_inoperative blockade of Elatea by Cassander [mainly] Olympiodorus mainly rendered Cassander's blockade of Elatea inoperative.

l: Callion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Callion, a place, is defended by Ætolians before Galati capture, plunder, burn, and massacre its people, inflicting atrocities, suicide, deprivation, and abuse on women and maidens.

l: Acichorius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Acichorius, Brennus’s colleague in the invasion of Greece, commands Galati and troops, leads a Celtic division during retreat, and joins Brennus’s fleeing forces after Ætolian attacks delay his division.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Greeks are an ancient population who, though dejected, are driven by danger to defend Greek liberty and security. They assemble an allied army at Thermopylæ against the Galatians, led by Athenians under Callippus and reinforced by contingents from Bœotia, Phocis, the Locrians, Megarians, Ætolians, Macedonians, and Syrians. They send picked light-armed soldiers and cavalry to guard the Sperchius, then fight at Thermopylæ.

l: Sperchius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sperchius is a river crossed by the Galatians. Greeks destroy its bridges and guard it to resist them, but Galatian troops cross elsewhere, forcing the Greek detachment back.

l: Galatian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Galatian invasion of Greece, during Anaxicrates' archonship, threatened Greek liberty and security. Greeks assembled allied forces at Thermopylæ to oppose the Galati. The invasion culminated in a march on Delphi; the Greeks defeated and harried the invaders in retreat, destroying them in Phocis and preventing their return.

l: battle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Seven days after the battle, a Galati force attempting to cross Mount Œta near Heraclea was defeated by the garrison under Telesarchus. Telesarchus fell during the action.

l: war against the other Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_expected_to_become easier [if Brennus forces the Ætolians back into Ætolia] Brennus thought that driving the Ætolians back into Ætolia would make the war against the other Greeks easier. His plan included sending a large Galati force into Ætolia and attacking the Greek position at Thermopylæ from the rear.

l: massacre at Callion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_avenged_by Ætolians [with severe losses inflicted on the Galati] The massacre at Callion was carried out by the Galati after they captured the town. They killed males, old men, and infants, abused women, and committed acts of cannibalism and sexual violence; the Ætolians responded by pursuing and attacking the retreating Galati.

l: panic among the Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The panic among the Galati began during the night after their retreat, when some thought they heard approaching horses and enemies. It spread through the host, and in the darkness the Galati mistook one another for Greeks and killed one another in large numbers.

l: Brennus’ suicide, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Brennus’ suicide followed his wounding and the destruction suffered by his army. Although his wounds were not mortal, he drank neat wine freely and killed himself, apparently from fear of his comrades or shame over the calamity he had caused.

l: The Seven Wise Men, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Seven Wise Men are a Greek-named group of seven sages: Thales, Bias, Pittacus, Cleobulus, Solon, Chilo, and, according to Plato, Myson instead of Periander. They came to Delphi, offered Apollo the sayings “Know thyself” and “Not too much of anything,” and inscribed them in the temple vestibule.

l: Solon of Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_from Athens [the Athenian] Solon advised the Amphictyones to consecrate the land around Cirrha to Apollo so that the god’s grove would extend to the sea. He also devised the plan of diverting the river Plistus and using hellebore to make its water disable the besieged people of Cirrha.

l: oracle concerning Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle concerning Homer foretells mixed fortune, identifies Ios as his motherland and receiver of his remains, and warns against young boys’ riddle; it ends with Homer’s grief and death after failing to solve fisher boys’ riddle.

l: Ios, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ios is identified by the oracle concerning Homer as the island that would receive Homer’s remains. Its inhabitants show Homer’s tomb and, elsewhere on the island, the tomb of Clymene, whom they say was Homer’s mother.

l: grave of Neoptolemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The grave of Neoptolemus lies in precincts to the left of the temple at Delphi. The people of Delphi perform annual funeral rites there.

l: Cassotis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cassotis is a walled fountain reached by an ascent through the wall near the temple at Delphi; its water runs underground, inspires Apollo’s sanctuary women with prophetic powers, and is named for a Nymph of Parnassus.

l: The Lounge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Lounge is a building above the fountain at Delphi, dedicated by the people of Cnidos, containing paintings by Polygnotus; formerly, the people of Delphi assembled there to discuss serious and trifling subjects.

l: Phrontis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phrontis, son of Onetor and Menelaus’s exceptionally able pilot, stands aboard Menelaus’s ship, then dies while sailing past Sunium in Attica; Menelaus remains to perform his funeral rites.

l: Nestor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Nestor sails with Menelaus until Menelaus remains behind after Phrontis’s death, praises Theseus and Pirithous as heroes, and is depicted wearing a hat, carrying a spear, beside a dust-rolling horse.

l: Lescheos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lescheos gives accounts of the deaths of Eioneus, Admetus, Coroebus, Priam, Axion, and Agenor. He says that Priam was killed at the palace doors rather than at the altar of Household Zeus, and that Coroebus was killed by Diomede.

l: Andromache, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_a_son Neoptolemus [the baby boy is said to have been killed by being hurled from a tower] Andromache is depicted among the Trojan women with a baby boy at her breast. Lescheos says that the baby was later hurled from a tower because of Neoptolemus’s private hatred, rather than by decree of the Greeks.

l: Polyxena, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_killed_at Achilles [at his tomb, according to the poets] Polyxena is depicted with her hair plaited in the manner of maidens. The poets say that she was slain at the tomb of Achilles, and the narrator has seen paintings of her death at Athens and Pergamus beyond the river Caicus.

l: the Trojan women, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: are_depicted_as captives [sadly dejected in the painting] The Trojan women in the painting look sorrowful and dejected, as if they are already captives. They include Andromache, Medesicaste, and Polyxena.

l: the painting of Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The painting of Polygnotus depicts the capture of Ilium and the Greeks’ return. It unfolds along a pebbled seashore, with Menelaus preparing to sail while companions descend, carry water, and dismantle tents. Helen is seated and admired, while Helenus is dejected; Briseis looks at Helen with Diomede and Iphis. The scene includes wounded warriors, Æthra with shaven head, Demophon considering her rescue, Andromache nursing a baby, Trojan women, and Nestor. It also shows Trojan dead, including Priam and Coroebus, Sinon and Anchialus carrying Laomedon’s corpse, and Antenor’s household loading belongings onto an ass with a child seated on it. A couplet identifies Polygnotus of Thasos as the painter.

l: Wooden Horse, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_depicted_above Troy [only its head appears above the walls] The Wooden Horse is represented by its head alone above the walls of Troy. It is painted near the figures associated with the fall of the city.

l: Ajax the son of Oileus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ajax the son of Oileus stands near an altar holding a shield and is bound by an oath concerning the violation of Cassandra, administered by the sons of Atreus. Later he appears wet with sea foam, like a shipwrecked man, watching others play dice and hating Odysseus for urging the Greeks to stone him.

l: altar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The altar appears in the scene involving Ajax and Cassandra, with Ajax standing near it and Cassandra holding the statue of Athene. Another altar is shown with a frightened little boy clinging to it and a brazen coat of mail lying upon it.

l: Antenor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_house house of Antenor Antenor’s house is depicted with a leopard’s skin over the porch as a sign to the Greeks not to harm his family. Antenor is shown standing near his daughter Crino, while his wife Theano and sons Glaucus and Eurymachus are also depicted.

l: captives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Captives are depicted between Æthra and Nestor, including Clymene, Creusa, Aristomache, and Xenodice; other named women recline above, and Laodice appears near the altar.

l: violation of Cassandra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The violation of Cassandra is the subject of an oath taken by Ajax the son of Oileus. Ajax stands near the altar with a shield while the sons of Atreus administer the oath.

l: Coroebus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Coroebus, Mygdon’s son, comes intending to marry Cassandra, but is killed, with accounts differing between Neoptolemus and Diomede.

l: Lescheos’s account of the Trojan dead, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lescheos’s account identifies Eioneus as slain by Neoptolemus, Admetus by Philoctetes, Coroebus by Diomede, Axion by Eurypylus, and Agenor by Neoptolemus. It also states that Priam was killed at the palace doors after being torn away from the altar.

l: incidents in the capture of Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The incidents include the deaths of Trojan figures, the removal of Laomedon’s corpse for burial, and the depiction of Antenor’s family under a sign warning the Greeks not to harm them. Simonides attributes their painting to Polygnotus of Thasos.

l: the painting, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The painting depicts scenes in Hades, including Odysseus’ descent, Charon’s boat on Acheron, and punishments for people who mistreated fathers or committed sacrilege. In its upper part are dice and Ajax the son of Oileus, looking at dice players, with Meleager above. Its lower part includes Hector, Thamyris, Memnon, and Sarpedon, with Paris and Penthesilea above. Elsewhere it shows Callisto, Sisyphus, Tantalus under a winejar, water carriers, birds on Memnon’s cloak, and a mockery of the Eleusinian mysteries.

l: picture (Polygnotus’ painting), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The picture represents Odysseus descending to Hades to consult Tiresias about returning home. Its left part contains Acheron, with reeds, ghostlike fishes, Charon, and his boat, alongside Tellis, Cleobœa, and figures suffering or honored. It then shows Ocnus, Ariadne and Phædra, Odysseus performing a rite, Theseus and Pirithous, and numerous other figures.

l: Acheron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Acheron is represented as a river in the painting, with reeds, indistinct fish, and Charon’s boat.

l: Charon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Charon, an old ferryman of the dead, rows a boat on Acheron and unwillingly admits living Theseus and Pirithous.

l: Cleobœa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cleobœa is a virgin depicted in Charon’s boat holding a cist used in Demeter’s worship; she came from Paros and first brought Demeter’s mysteries to Thasos.

l: sacrilegious wretch, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: suffers punishment of the sacrilegious wretch [in Hades] The sacrilegious wretch is depicted near the man who mistreated his father, suffering punishment in Hades.

l: punishment of the sacrilegious wretch, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The punishment of the sacrilegious wretch is represented in Polygnotus’ painting. A woman who appears familiar with poison and other harmful things is shown punishing him.

l: piety to the gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Piety to the gods is illustrated by Athenians at the temple of Olympian Zeus, Datis toward Delians and Apollo’s statue, and Polygnotus’ punished sacrilegious wretch, reflecting earlier honor for deity.

l: Eurynomus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Eurynomus is a demon in Hades, as described by the Antiquarians at Delphi. It eats dead flesh clean to the bones and, in a painting, appears blueish-black, fang-showing, and seated on a vulture’s skin; it is absent from named poems.

l: Ocnus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ocnus is a seated man who industriously makes rope, only for a she-ass to eat it as fast as he makes it; his labor brings no profit because his extravagant wife spends what he gathers.

l: daughters of Pandareus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The daughters of Pandareus, Camiro and Clytie, were orphaned when their parents died through divine wrath. Aphrodite and other goddesses nurtured and gifted them, before Harpies carried them to the Furies; they are painted crowned with flowers, playing dice.

l: Pandareus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pandareus, a Milesian from Cretan Miletus, associates with Tantalus in theft and perjury and fathers Camiro and Clytie.

l: Iaseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Iaseus is Phocus’ closest friend, offering gifts and a gold-set stone signet-ring; he is depicted taking it from Phocus’ hand as their friendship’s memorial.

l: Palamedes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Palamedes invents dice, is depicted playing them with Actæon, Salaminian Ajax, and Thersites without a beard, and is drowned while fishing by Diomede and Odysseus.

l: Memnon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Memnon, a bearded king of the Ethiopians, came to Ilium from Susa in Persia and the river Choaspes. In a painting he sits beside Hector near Sarpedon, touching Sarpedon’s shoulder, cloaked in Memnonides birds that annually tend his tomb near the Hellespont.
